conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/name: The French Wars of Religion and St Bartholomew's Day
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/religi: Older historians saw the wars mainly as a struggle among great noble houses — Guise, Bourbon and Montmorency — for control of a weak crown, with religion as a cloak. Since the 1970s Natalie Zemon Davis, Denis Crouzet, Barbara Diefendorf and Mack Holt have shown that religion was central: Catholics and Huguenots believed the other side's worship polluted the community and invited God's wrath, and popular violence took ritual forms. Noble faction, royal minorities, fiscal crisis and Spanish intervention all mattered, but they were channelled through confessional allegiance.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/sides/: Catholic party and the Catholic League
Catholic Spain and the Papacy; Protestant England and German princes
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/summar: Between 1562 and 1598 France was torn by eight civil wars between Catholics and Protestant Huguenots, inflamed by noble rivalries, royal weakness and foreign intervention. The worst episode, the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572, killed thousands of Protestants in Paris and the provinces. The wars ended when the Protestant Henry of Navarre became king, converted to Catholicism and issued the Edict of Nantes (1598), granting Huguenots limited toleration.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/story:
From the 1550s Calvin's Geneva trained and sent pastors into France, and by 1562 there were perhaps 1,500 to 2,000 Reformed congregations and as many as two million Huguenots, about a tenth of the population, including a third or more of the nobility. Their first national synod met secretly in Paris in 1559. That year Henry II, who had vowed to extirpate heresy, died after a jousting accident, leaving the throne to his sickly sons Francis II and Charles IX and real power to their mother, Catherine de' Medici, and to competing noble factions: the Catholic Guise family, the Bourbon princes (Navarre and Condé), who led the Protestants, and the Montmorency clan. A Huguenot plot to seize the young king at Amboise in 1560 was savagely suppressed. Catherine and her chancellor Michel de L'Hospital sought reconciliation at the Colloquy of Poissy (1561) and, in the Edict of January 1562, permitted Protestant worship outside towns.

On 1 March 1562, at Wassy in Champagne, the Duke of Guise's men attacked a Protestant congregation worshipping in a barn, killing about fifty and wounding many more. Condé took up arms, Huguenots seized Orléans, Lyon, Rouen and other towns, and iconoclasts smashed images while Catholics massacred Protestants in Sens, Toulouse and elsewhere. The first war saw the battle of Dreux (December 1562) and the assassination of Francis of Guise by a Huguenot, Poltrot de Méré, in February 1563; the Edict of Amboise brought a short peace. A second war began in 1567 with a Huguenot attempt to seize the king at Meaux, and at Nîmes on Michaelmas 1567 Protestants massacred Catholic clergy and notables in the ‘Michelade’. In the third war Condé was killed after the battle of Jarnac (1569), and the Peace of Saint-Germain (1570) gave Huguenots four security towns, including La Rochelle.

To seal the peace Catherine arranged the marriage of her daughter Marguerite to the Protestant Henry of Navarre in Paris on 18 August 1572. Four days later Admiral Coligny was wounded by an assassin. Fearing Huguenot revenge, the king's council decided to eliminate the Protestant leaders; in the early hours of 24 August, St Bartholomew's Day, the Duke of Guise's men killed Coligny, and the killing of the Huguenot nobles in the Louvre and their lodgings set off a popular massacre in which Parisian militiamen and crowds slaughtered Protestant men, women and children for several days, throwing many bodies into the Seine. The killings spread to Meaux, Orléans, Lyon, Rouen, Toulouse, Bordeaux and other towns into October. Pope Gregory XIII had a Te Deum sung and a medal struck; Philip II of Spain is said to have laughed for the only time; Protestant Europe was horrified. Henry of Navarre survived by abjuring his faith under duress.

The massacre transformed the Huguenots. Thousands abjured or emigrated, and the movement contracted into its strongholds in the south and west, but the survivors resisted fiercely — La Rochelle withstood a royal siege in 1573 — and their writers, including Theodore Beza, François Hotman and the anonymous author of the Vindiciae contra tyrannos (1579), developed theories of legitimate resistance to tyrants. Henry III made concessions in the Peace of Monsieur (1576), provoking Catholic nobles and towns to form the Catholic League. When the death of the king's last brother in 1584 made the Protestant Henry of Navarre heir to the throne, the League revived under Henry of Guise, allied with Philip II in the Treaty of Joinville (December 1584), and demanded the exclusion of a heretic king.

In the ‘War of the Three Henrys’ the League dominated Paris, which rose against Henry III on the Day of the Barricades (12 May 1588). The king took revenge by having Henry of Guise and his brother the cardinal murdered at Blois on 23–24 December 1588. League preachers denounced him as a tyrant, the Sorbonne released his subjects from obedience, and on 1 August 1589 the Dominican friar Jacques Clément stabbed him at Saint-Cloud. Henry of Navarre, now Henry IV, won battles at Arques (1589) and Ivry (1590) but could not take Catholic Paris, whose people endured a terrible siege and famine in 1590 before Spanish troops under the Duke of Parma relieved it.

On 25 July 1593 Henry IV abjured Protestantism at Saint-Denis — whether he said ‘Paris is well worth a Mass’ is doubtful — and in March 1594 he entered Paris. Pope Clement VIII absolved him in 1595, the League disintegrated, and war with Spain ended with the Peace of Vervins (May 1598). In April 1598 Henry signed the Edict of Nantes, which granted Huguenots freedom of conscience, public worship in specified places, civil equality and some hundred and fifty places of refuge and security garrisons, while restoring Catholic worship everywhere.

The settlement did not end religious hostility. Henry IV was murdered by the Catholic zealot François Ravaillac in 1610. Renewed Huguenot risings in the 1620s ended with the fall of La Rochelle (1628) and the Peace of Alès (1629), which removed their military privileges, and in 1685 Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes, driving some 150,000–200,000 Huguenots into exile and provoking the Camisard revolt in the Cévennes.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/nameOf: Both sides believed they were purging the kingdom of pollution and averting God's wrath. Catholic preachers called heretics a cancer and a plague, and crowds treated the massacre of Huguenots as a rite of purification, sometimes rebaptising Protestant children in Catholic blood. Huguenots smashed images and Mass vessels as idolatry and sang Psalms, notably Psalm 68 (‘Let God arise, let his enemies be scattered’), as their battle hymn. The Catholic League swore an oath to defend the holy Catholic, apostolic and Roman Church, organised penitential processions in white, and celebrated Henry III's assassin as a martyr. Pius V urged Charles IX to show no mercy to heretics and sent papal troops in 1569; Gregory XIII commemorated St Bartholomew with a medal reading ‘Ugonottorum strages’ (slaughter of the Huguenots) and frescoes by Vasari in the Vatican.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/religi: The rapid growth of the Reformed churches, organised by Geneva, which by 1562 included perhaps a tenth of the French population and a large part of the nobility.
Catholic belief that the toleration of heresy would bring divine punishment on the whole kingdom, and Huguenot conviction that the Mass was idolatry.
The tradition of the ‘Most Christian King’ consecrated at Reims and sworn to expel heretics, which made a Protestant succession unthinkable to many Catholics.
The apocalyptic anxieties traced by Denis Crouzet, which led Catholics to see violence against heretics as a sacred duty.
Iconoclasm and the seizure of churches by Huguenots, and Catholic massacres of Protestants, which created cycles of sacred revenge.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/otherC: Royal weakness after Henry II's death in 1559, with a succession of child or childless kings and a regent mother.
Rivalry between the great noble houses of Guise, Bourbon and Montmorency for power at court.
The crown's fiscal crisis after the Habsburg–Valois wars and the demobilisation of thousands of soldiers in 1559.
Spanish intervention to prevent a Protestant France, and English and German Protestant support for the Huguenots.
Local rivalries in towns and provinces, in which confession mapped onto existing factions.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/trigge: The massacre of a Protestant congregation by the Duke of Guise's men at Wassy on 1 March 1562.
The attempted assassination of Admiral Coligny on 22 August 1572, which precipitated the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.
The death of Francis, Duke of Anjou, in 1584, which made the Protestant Henry of Navarre heir to the throne.

Died in January 1589 at Blois, weeks after the murder of Guise; her reputation was blackened by Protestant polemic.
Admiral of France and Huguenot leader

Murdered at the start of the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre.

conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/casual: Commonly cited estimates for all deaths related to the wars from 1562 to 1598 — including famine, plague and the destruction of harvests as well as battle and massacre — range from about 2 to 4 million, though these are rough extrapolations from local evidence and some historians regard them as too high. For the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre, most historians estimate about 2,000–3,000 killed in Paris and a further 3,000–7,000 in the provinces, giving roughly 5,000–10,000; contemporary Protestant martyrologies gave higher figures.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/effect: The Bourbon dynasty came to the throne, and France emerged from the wars with a strengthened monarchy that later developed into absolutism.
The Edict of Nantes created a legal, if limited and unequal, coexistence of two confessions in one kingdom.
Political theorists, from the Huguenot monarchomachs to Jean Bodin and the politiques, developed new ideas of resistance, sovereignty and the state's priority over confessional unity.
The wars devastated many regions through repeated campaigns, sieges, famine and plague.
French Protestantism, after peaking around 1562, shrank to a minority of about 1 million concentrated in the south and west.
The Catholic League's militancy fed into the Catholic Reformation in France, with new religious orders and devotional movements in the early seventeenth century.
St Bartholomew became a defining memory of martyrdom for Reformed Protestants everywhere and a lasting charge against the papacy.
The idea that a king's religion should determine his subjects' faith was challenged, but survived until the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/legacy: The French Wars of Religion became, with St Bartholomew's Day, Europe's archetypal warning against religious civil war, cited by Voltaire, the Enlightenment and later advocates of secular toleration. The Edict of Nantes is often remembered as a milestone of religious liberty, though it was a pragmatic truce rather than a principle. In 1997 Pope John Paul II, in Paris for World Youth Day, expressed regret for the massacre.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/dissen: In his Counsel to Desolate France (1562), written as the first war began, he urged both Catholics and Protestants to stop forcing consciences, saying each side's persecution of the other was the root of the kingdom's misery.

At the Estates-General of Orléans in 1560 he pleaded: ‘Let us do away with these diabolical names, Lutherans, Huguenots and papists, which are the names of parties and sedition; let us not change the name of Christians.’

A Catholic magistrate and essayist who criticised the cruelty of religious zeal on both sides, comparing French tortures unfavourably with the customs of Brazilian ‘cannibals’ and praising Julian the Apostate's freedom of conscience (Essays, 1580).
According to a tradition first recorded later, he refused to allow the massacre of Protestants in his diocese in 1572, and Lisieux saw no killings.
conflicts/french-wars-of-religion/campai: The spread of the St Bartholomew's massacres
Catholic militias, crowds and local authorities

From Paris on 24 August the killings spread as news and rumours of royal orders arrived: to Meaux and Orléans within days, to Lyon at the end of August, to Rouen in mid-September and to Bordeaux and Toulouse in early October.
Henry IV and the royalist and Huguenot army

Proclaimed king at Saint-Cloud after Henry III's murder, Henry IV retreated to Normandy, defeated the League at Arques and Ivry, besieged Paris without success in 1590, and finally won the capital by abjuring Protestantism at Saint-Denis and entering Paris in March 1594.
